whatItIs: Not "plain-language rules." It is a writing-skill plugin (Claude Code + Codex + agentskills.io) wrapping ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, shipped together with a real Python evaluation harness (~50 KB of code across evals/ and tools/), about 400 committed raw model generations, a CI gate that recomputes every published README number from those raw files, and a committed self-refutation that retracted its own headline metric. The prescriptive part is ordinary. The measurement apparatus around it is the unusual part, and it is better engineered than most.
method: `skills/simple-english/SKILL.md` (7.7 KB, author says ~1,700 tokens) splits writing into two registers. The Document register is 12 numbered rules: classify each passage procedural (imperative, 20 words/sentence) or descriptive (simple tenses, 25 words, 6 sentences/paragraph); never touch code, identifiers, flags, quoted errors or facts; condition before command with a comma; simple tenses and active voice, no present perfect, no "-ing" clause after a comma; modals restricted to can/will/must with should/would/may/might/could banned outright; keep articles and "that" ("STE is short, not terse"); no semicolons or em-dashes; one word one meaning document-wide (`make sure that` replaces check/verify/confirm/validate/ensure, `configuration` replaces config/settings/options, noun chains over three words broken with a preposition); define each concept term under ten words at first use; state the fact not its importance; no bold lead-ins or headings under three sentences. The Reply register is 7 rules governing the chat turn itself: prose only, five sentences maximum with list items counted, first sentence answers, no em-dashes, no contractions, no openers or closers. Then a "Self-Check Before You Deliver" section that tells the model to grep its own draft for literal strings — `—`, `**`, `#`, `has been`, `should`, `;`, `, making`, `check`, `config` — and fix each hit. Two modes: Plain by default, Strict only when the user names STE/ASD-STE100/compliance, which loads `references/strict-vocabulary.md`; the reply stays Plain in every mode. The 53 numbered Issue 9 rules live out of the hot path in `references/rule-catalog.md` (10 KB, 9 sections, paraphrased with software examples) and load only for CHECK mode, where the skill forbids citing a rule number from memory — a direct response to a recorded baseline failure in which the agent invented "Rule 3.1" and "Rule 4.2". The same rule block ships four ways (skill, `prompts/system-prompt.md`, `output-styles/simple-english.md`, and two hooks in `src/hooks/`), and CI asserts the four copies have not drifted.
measures: Yes — more than any writing repo I have read — but it measures the generator's text surface, never a reader's understanding. Three layers, all real and all reproducible. (1) `evals/ste_lint.py:84` `lint()` is a deterministic regex counter over 11 categories (sentence_over_limit, contraction, banned_modal, perfect_tense, ing_clause, semicolon, em_dash, latin_abbrev, slop_word, trailing_condition, synonym_rotation), normalised to violations per 100 words, with a 45-line `self_test()` of adversarial fixtures (tables, bullet lists, bold-label lists, seven kinds of dash) and an honest docstring ceiling: "a regex pass, not a grammar parser... not a compliance verdict." (2) `evals/ste_lint.py:185` `reader_check()` counts what a reader sees in a reply: sentences with list items and table rows forced to count, over_cap beyond 5, em-dashes, bold spans, headers, bullets, contractions, summed into `visible_total`. (3) `evals/check_numbers.py` recomputes every number printed in the README from the committed raw generations and exits 1 on the first mismatch; `.github/workflows/check.yml` runs it on every push. Harness: `evals/run_reply_bench.py:38` shells `claude -p --setting-sources "" --disallowedTools Bash,Read,Write,... --effort low`, one file per condition×scenario, resumable, skipping harness error strings. Eight reply scenarios (`evals/reply_scenarios.json`, each carrying a jargon term) and eight document scenarios (`evals/scenarios.json`, each tagged procedural or descriptive). Blind pairwise judging runs both orders and averages to cancel position bias (`evals/run_bench.py:250`). The decisive negative result is committed: `evals/results/WHY-USELESS-2026-09-02.md` reports that an 8-line prompt (`evals/results/rebuild-2026-09-02/micro-prompt.txt`, 299 bytes) beat the full 50-rule skill on every reader-visible metric — 5.8 sentences vs 13.4, 2 em-dashes vs 17, zero bold/headers/bullets vs 24/3/22 — while *losing* on the skill's own linter, and names the cause: "the skill optimizes for evals/ste_lint.py, and 50+ rules dilute the 5 that matter." The limit is the one that matters to us: nowhere in the repo is a question asked of a document. No answer key, no code-derived ground truth, no comprehension score — I grepped all five runner scripts for answer_key/comprehen/quiz/question and the only hit was a regex matching the filler opener "great question". The judge rubric (`run_bench.py:253`) asks a model for a 0-10 opinion on whether "a tired non-native reader can misread any sentence"; no reader is ever simulated and nothing is ever got right or wrong. So: it measures its own prompt's effect on output form, rigorously. It does not measure whether a document works.

transferable.approach: A CI gate that recomputes every number printed in the prose from committed raw data and fails the build on a mismatch — the mechanised half of terse's "lie" failure class, with no model call in the loop. `expect(label, text, pattern, value)` regexes a claim out of the README and compares it to a value recomputed from the raw files; `versions()` asserts the version string in SKILL.md, three manifests and the README badge are one value; `sync()` asserts the rule block duplicated across three files has not drifted and still contains seven load-bearing phrases.

transferable.whyItMightWork: terse's audit derives an answer key from the code and pays a fresh model per question to catch lies. A whole class of lies — stale numbers, stale versions, drifted duplicated blocks — is catchable deterministically, for free, and as a gate rather than a report. It also inverts cheaply: the audit can emit a check_numbers-shaped script as a deliverable, so the document stays true after the audit agent goes away. 174 lines, stdlib only, no dependency on anything ASD-STE100.
transferable.collidesWith: Nothing. It is orthogonal to all four revise passes and sits beside audit's lie class rather than inside it. Closest tension: it is a CI gate, and terse rejected CI punctuation gates — but the rejection was of gating on style opinion, and this gates on arithmetic, which is a different object.

transferable.approach: Metric-design discipline: when a metric is defined, name and close the loophole the previous metric left. The old reply cap said "code blocks and list items do not count", so the model bulleted everything and scored clean; `reader_check()` forces every list item and table row to count as a sentence, and `self_test()` pins the behaviour with a fixture asserting exactly (5 sentences, 1 em-dash, 1 bold, 1 header, 2 bullets).
transferable.whereItLives: evals/ste_lint.py:185-214 (reader_check), :203 the split that strips markdown before counting, :240 the fixture assertion; loophole diagnosed at evals/results/WHY-USELESS-2026-09-02.md item 3
transferable.whyItMightWork: terse's audit scores "right answers" and classifies failures as lie/placement/findability. Each of those labels has an exploitable edge the writer can optimise toward — e.g. moving a fact into a heading so a keyword search finds it without the prose ever saying it. Committing an adversarial fixture per failure class, the way self_test() does, makes the classifier's own loopholes visible before a bake-off optimises into them.
transferable.collidesWith: Partly overlaps audit's failure-classification step: it would add a fixture suite under that step rather than replace it. No contradiction.

One paragraph (299 bytes, 8 lines) against the full 53-rule ASD-STE100 skill across 8 scenarios: the micro prompt won on sentences, em-dashes, bold, headers and bullets, and lost only on the linter the standard itself defines.

weaknesses: The headline is still a form metric wearing a reader's name. `reader_check()` is called "what a reader sees", but it counts em-dashes, bold spans, headers, bullets and sentence count — typography, not comprehension. The 2026-09-02 audit correctly convicted the old linter of measuring "grammar obedience, not readability", then replaced it with a metric that measures formatting obedience. Nobody in this repository ever asks whether a document answered a question, and that is precisely the gap terse fills; nothing here closes it. Second, the provenance of slop.tsv is unverifiable in-repo: "words named by 8 or more of 122 published ban lists" appears exactly once, in a docstring at evals/ste_lint.py:40-41, with no source list, no collection script and no citation committed — I grepped README, CHANGELOG, word-swaps.md and the results pages and found nothing. The column of counts is therefore an assertion, in a repo whose own CI exists to stop exactly that. Third, statistical power is thin and the repo says so: one generation per cell for documents, two runs for replies, "one run moves by about 0.5 on this model", one judge model from the same family as the judged text, 32 of 72 judge files pre-dating the effort pin. Fourth, the flagship rule does not hold — the five-sentence cap is met in 5 of 16 sonnet replies, admitted as "the weakest rule". Fifth, the PostToolUse hook lints every .md the agent writes and exits 2 to push the violation list back into context: an automatic style-nag loop on all Markdown in the session, which is the rejected prose-linter pattern plus a token cost the audit itself priced at ~5.9k cached tokens per session. Sixth, an attribution honesty note rather than a defect: the repo retains 53 rules and a 12-rule document register after measuring that its own 8-line control beat them, because the standard is its identity. terse has no such constraint and should not inherit the conclusion, only the data.
